normative.obligation: The third field is a 16-bit protocol type whose value in an Address Resolution packet is ether_type$ADDRESS_RESOLUTION.

normative.obligation: The fields that follow constitute the Ethernet packet data carried by the Address Resolution protocol.

normative.quote:
16.bit: (ar$hrd) Hardware address space (e.g., Ethernet,

16.bit: (ar$pro) Protocol address space.  For Ethernet

normative.quote: 8.bit: (ar$hln) byte length of each hardware address
normative.obligation: The third packet-data field is an 8-bit ar$hln giving the byte length of each hardware address in the packet.

nbytes: (ar$tha) Hardware address of target of this

normative.obligation: The ninth and last packet-data field is ar$tpa, holding the target's protocol address and occupying the number of bytes given by ar$pln.

normative.quote: In the case of the 10Mbit Ethernet, address resolution is needed and some lower layer (probably the hardware driver) must consult the Address Resolution module (perhaps implemented in the Ethernet support module) to convert the <protocol type, target protocol address> pair to a 48.bit Ethernet address.
normative.obligation: Before transmitting on 10Mbit Ethernet, a lower layer must consult the Address Resolution module to convert the <protocol type, target protocol address> pair into a 48-bit Ethernet address.

normative.quote: The Address Resolution module tries to find this pair in a table.
normative.obligation: On being consulted, the Address Resolution module looks the <protocol type, target protocol address> pair up in its translation table.

normative.quote: If it finds the pair, it gives the corresponding 48.bit Ethernet address back to the caller (hardware driver)
normative.obligation: When the lookup succeeds, the module returns the 48-bit Ethernet address stored against that pair to the caller.

normative.quote: which then transmits the packet.
normative.obligation: Having received a 48-bit Ethernet address from the module, the caller transmits the pending packet.

normative.quote: If it does not, it probably informs the caller that it is throwing the packet away
normative.obligation: When the lookup fails, the module informs the caller that the packet is being discarded.

normative.quote: it is throwing the packet away (on the assumption the packet will be retransmitted by a higher network layer)
normative.obligation: When the lookup fails, the module discards the packet that prompted the resolution rather than queueing it.

normative.quote: and generates an Ethernet packet with a type field of ether_type$ADDRESS_RESOLUTION.
normative.obligation: When the lookup fails, the module generates an Ethernet packet whose type field is ether_type$ADDRESS_RESOLUTION.

normative.quote: The Address Resolution module then sets the ar$hrd field to ares_hrd$Ethernet
normative.obligation: In the generated request, the module sets ar$hrd to ares_hrd$Ethernet.

normative.quote: ar$pro to the protocol type that is being resolved
normative.obligation: In the generated request, the module sets ar$pro to the protocol type whose address is being resolved.

normative.quote: ar$hln to 6 (the number of bytes in a 48.bit Ethernet address)
normative.obligation: In the generated request, the module sets ar$hln to 6, the byte length of a 48-bit Ethernet address.

normative.quote: ar$pln to the length of an address in that protocol
normative.obligation: In the generated request, the module sets ar$pln to the byte length of an address in the protocol being resolved.

normative.quote: ar$op to ares_op$REQUEST
normative.obligation: In the generated request, the module sets ar$op to ares_op$REQUEST.

normative.quote: ar$sha with the 48.bit ethernet address of itself
normative.obligation: In the generated request, the module fills ar$sha with its own 48-bit Ethernet address.

normative.quote: ar$spa with the protocol address of itself
normative.obligation: In the generated request, the module fills ar$spa with its own protocol address.

normative.quote: and ar$tpa with the protocol address of the machine that is trying to be accessed.
normative.obligation: In the generated request, the module fills ar$tpa with the protocol address of the machine it is trying to reach.

normative.quote: It does not set ar$tha to anything in particular, because it is this value that it is trying to determine.
normative.obligation: In the generated request the sender leaves ar$tha unconstrained, placing no particular value in it.

normative.quote: It could set ar$tha to the broadcast address for the hardware (all ones in the case of the 10Mbit Ethernet) if that makes it convenient for some aspect of the implementation.
normative.obligation: The sender is permitted to set ar$tha in a request to the hardware broadcast address, which on 10Mbit Ethernet is all ones.

normative.quote: It then causes this packet to be broadcast to all stations on the Ethernet cable originally determined by the routing mechanism.
normative.obligation: The module broadcasts the generated request to all stations on the cable that routing selected for the original packet.

normative.quote: When an address resolution packet is received, the receiving Ethernet module gives the packet to the Address Resolution module which goes through an algorithm similar to the following.
normative.obligation: On receiving an address resolution packet, the Ethernet module hands it to the Address Resolution module, which processes it by the algorithm that follows.

normative.quote: Negative conditionals indicate an end of processing and a discarding of the packet.
normative.obligation: Whenever any guard in the reception algorithm evaluates false, the receiver ends processing and discards the packet.

normative.quote: ?Do I have the hardware type in ar$hrd?
normative.obligation: The receiver tests whether it implements the hardware type named in ar$hrd before processing the packet further.

normative.quote: [optionally check the hardware length ar$hln]
normative.obligation: The receiver is permitted, but not required, to check the hardware address length in ar$hln for consistency.

normative.quote: ?Do I speak the protocol in ar$pro?
normative.obligation: The receiver tests whether it speaks the protocol named in ar$pro before processing the packet further.

normative.quote: [optionally check the protocol length ar$pln]
normative.obligation: The receiver is permitted, but not required, to check the protocol address length in ar$pln for consistency.

normative.quote: Merge_flag := false
normative.obligation: The receiver initialises Merge_flag to false before examining the translation table.

normative.quote:
If the pair <protocol type, sender protocol address> is

	hardware address field of the entry with the new
	information in the packet
normative.obligation: If the <protocol type, sender protocol address> pair is already in the translation table, the receiver overwrites that entry's sender hardware address with the one carried in the packet.

normative.quote: and set Merge_flag to true.
normative.obligation: If an existing entry was updated, the receiver sets Merge_flag to true.

normative.quote: ?Am I the target protocol address?
normative.obligation: The receiver tests whether ar$tpa names its own protocol address before processing the packet further.

normative.quote:
If Merge_flag is false, add the triplet <protocol type,

normative.obligation: When the receiver is the target and no existing entry was merged, it adds the <protocol type, sender protocol address, sender hardware address> triplet to its translation table.

normative.quote: ?Is the opcode ares_op$REQUEST?  (NOW look at the opcode!!)
normative.obligation: Only after the table has been updated does the receiver test whether ar$op is ares_op$REQUEST.

Swap hardware and protocol fields, putting the local
	    hardware and protocol addresses in the sender fields.
normative.obligation: To build the reply, the receiver swaps the sender and target hardware and protocol fields so that its own hardware and protocol addresses occupy the sender fields.

normative.quote: Set the ar$op field to ares_op$REPLY
normative.obligation: In the reply, the receiver sets ar$op to ares_op$REPLY.

normative.quote: Send the packet to the (new) target hardware address
normative.obligation: The receiver sends the reply to the new target hardware address, that is, the requester's hardware address, rather than broadcasting it.

normative.quote: on the same hardware on which the request was received.
normative.obligation: The receiver sends the reply out on the same piece of hardware on which the request arrived.

normative.quote: Notice that the <protocol type, sender protocol address, sender hardware address> triplet is merged into the table before the opcode is looked at.
normative.obligation: The receiver must merge the sender triplet into its translation table before it inspects the opcode, not afterwards.

normative.quote: Generalization:  The ar$hrd and ar$hln fields allow this protocol and packet format to be used for non-10Mbit Ethernets.
normative.obligation: An implementation carries the hardware medium in ar$hrd and its address length in ar$hln so that the same packet format serves hardware other than 10Mbit Ethernet.

normative.quote: For the 10Mbit Ethernet <ar$hrd, ar$hln> takes on the value <1, 6>.
normative.obligation: On 10Mbit Ethernet an implementation sets ar$hrd to 1 and ar$hln to 6.

normative.quote: For other hardware networks, the ar$pro field may no longer correspond to the Ethernet type field,
normative.obligation: On hardware other than Ethernet, an implementation is permitted to use ar$pro values that are not Ethernet type field values.

normative.quote: but it should be associated with the protocol whose address resolution is being sought.
normative.obligation: Whatever value space is used, ar$pro should identify the protocol whose address resolution is being sought.

normative.section: Why is it done this way??
normative.quote: This format allows the packet buffer to be reused if a reply is generated;
normative.obligation: A receiver is permitted to build the reply in the buffer that held the received request rather than allocating a new one.

normative.section: Why is it done this way??
normative.quote: a reply has the same length as a request, and several of the fields are the same.
normative.obligation: A reply packet has the same length as the request that provoked it.

normative.section: Why is it done this way??
normative.quote: The value of the hardware field (ar$hrd) is taken from a list for this purpose.  Currently the only defined value is for the 10Mbit Ethernet (ares_hrd$Ethernet = 1).
normative.obligation: An implementation draws ar$hrd from the assigned list of hardware values, of which ares_hrd$Ethernet = 1 is currently the only defined member.

normative.section: Why is it done this way??
normative.quote: The opcode is to determine if this is a request (which may cause a reply) or a reply to a previous request.
normative.obligation: The ar$op field denotes whether the packet is a request or a reply to a previous request, and a receiver takes it to mean exactly that.

normative.section: Why is it done this way??
normative.quote: a request (which may cause a reply)
normative.obligation: A request may provoke a reply, so a sender must tolerate receiving one and a receiver is permitted to produce one.

normative.section: Why is it done this way??
normative.quote: It has no meaning in the request form, since it is this number that the machine is requesting.
normative.obligation: In a request, ar$tha carries no meaning, so a receiver may not read any significance into its contents.

normative.section: Why is it done this way??
normative.quote: Its meaning in the reply form is the address of the machine making the request.
normative.obligation: In a reply, ar$tha holds the hardware address of the machine that made the request.

normative.section: Why is it done this way??
normative.quote: In some implementations (which do not get to look at the 14.byte ethernet header, for example) this may save some register shuffling or stack space by sending this field to the hardware driver as the hardware destination address of the packet.
normative.obligation: An implementation is permitted to pass ar$tha to the hardware driver as the packet's hardware destination address.

normative.section: Why is it done this way??
normative.quote: There are no padding bytes between addresses.
normative.obligation: An implementation inserts no padding bytes between the address fields of the packet.

normative.section: Why is it done this way??
normative.quote: The packet data should be viewed as a byte stream in which only 3 byte pairs are defined to be words (ar$hrd, ar$pro and ar$op)
normative.obligation: An implementation treats the packet data as a byte stream in which only ar$hrd, ar$pro and ar$op are word-sized fields.

normative.section: Why is it done this way??
normative.quote: which are sent most significant byte first (Ethernet/PDP-10 byte style).
normative.obligation: The three word fields ar$hrd, ar$pro and ar$op are transmitted most significant byte first.

normative.quote: In fact, it is not necessary for the monitor to speak any of the higher level protocols involved.
normative.obligation: A monitor is not required to implement any of the higher level protocols whose address resolution traffic it records.

normative.quote: When a monitor receives an Address Resolution packet, it always enters the <protocol type, sender protocol address, sender hardware address> in a table.
normative.obligation: A monitor enters the <protocol type, sender protocol address, sender hardware address> triplet of every Address Resolution packet it receives into its table, unconditionally.

normative.quote: It can determine the length of the hardware and protocol address from the ar$hln and ar$pln fields of the packet.
normative.obligation: A monitor may take the hardware and protocol address lengths of a packet it cannot otherwise interpret from its ar$hln and ar$pln fields.

normative.quote: If the opcode is a REPLY the monitor can then throw the packet away.
normative.obligation: Once it has recorded the sender triplet, a monitor is permitted to discard a packet whose opcode is REPLY.

normative.quote: If the opcode is a REQUEST and the target protocol address matches the protocol address of the monitor, the monitor sends a REPLY as it normally would.
normative.obligation: When a received REQUEST targets the monitor's own protocol address, the monitor replies exactly as an ordinary station would.

normative.quote: The monitor could try sending its own REQUEST,
normative.obligation: A monitor is permitted to originate its own REQUEST packets in order to collect more mappings.

normative.quote: but this could get two monitors into a REQUEST sending loop, and care must be taken.
normative.obligation: A monitor that originates REQUESTs must guard against entering an endless REQUEST-sending loop with another monitor.

normative.quote: Because the protocol and opcode are not combined into one field, the monitor does not need to know which request opcode is associated with which reply opcode for the same higher level protocol.
normative.obligation: A monitor is not required to know any per-protocol association between request and reply opcodes.

normative.quote: The length fields should also give enough information to enable it to "parse" a protocol addresses, although it has no knowledge of what the protocol addresses mean.
normative.obligation: A monitor may use the length fields alone to delimit the protocol addresses in a packet without understanding what those addresses mean.

normative.quote: Because requests are broadcast a monitor will receive the packet and can display it for debugging if desired.
normative.obligation: A monitor is permitted to display a received broadcast request for debugging purposes.
